title: PortLog harness as the provider-neutral process platform
description:
## Destination

Produce an implementation-ready specification for narrowing apps/server around the PortLog harness: every agent-initiated operation runs through one provider/model-agnostic harness; projects, threads, SQLite, WebSocket delivery, settings, and durable history remain server infrastructure; model choice is a global app default applied per turn; provider credentials remain harness configuration.

## Notes

Planning-only wayfinder effort. Consult domain-modeling and grilling for unresolved product vocabulary. Research agent harnesses, Palantir Ontology/AIP, Pi/OMP, and durable execution patterns when needed. Do not make the model emit a universal operation-kind taxonomy unless a later decision proves it necessary. Human approval is not mandatory by default; autonomous authority is bounded by scoped capabilities, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, recovery, and audit.

## Decisions so far

- [Define the provider-neutral turn and harness session boundary](pl-217.1) — Threads are provider-agnostic durable identities; each user turn is a durable harness task run by an on-demand PortLog invocation, with persisted events and execution state used for recovery. Completion is policy-evaluated; no universal HarnessOperationKind.
- [Define the canonical harness event and operation trace](pl-217.2) — Use typed model/tool/logic_program invocations with durable semantic boundaries, replay and retry rules, rebuildable projections, and optional raw diagnostics rather than raw payloads by default.
- [Specify provider and settings migration to per-turn harness routing](pl-217.4) — Clean-slate target: global resolved model selection routes every turn through PortLog; invocation metadata preserves the execution snapshot, while threads remain provider-neutral.
- [Research autonomous PortLog authority without mandatory human approvals](pl-217.6) — Approval-free execution is bounded by scoped capabilities/identity, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, durable recovery, and audit; escalation remains optional.
- [Define harness authority, approvals, and infrastructure ownership](pl-217.5) — PortLog owns the complete agent loop and capability authority; server remains infrastructure and adapter layer; generic tools use declared capability scope and policy metadata instead of a premature domain ontology.
- [Define governed PortLog process actions versus discovered tools](pl-217.3) — Start with generic registry-backed tools; defer governed domain actions until a concrete capability needs stronger semantics.
- [Define WebSocket and UI projection for harness traces](pl-217.7) — Follow OMP: conversation-first UI with inline expandable activity; durable typed events drive projections, transient deltas stream live, and reconnect rebuilds from SQLite/event log.

## Not yet specified

<!-- no remaining specified frontier; future domain-action work graduates only when a concrete capability requires it -->

## Out of scope

- Rebuilding the Paper chat design.
- Deleting the apps/server infrastructure spine.
- Treating Claude, Codex, OpenCode, or any other provider session as a product concept.

title: Define the provider-neutral turn and harness session boundary
description: ## Question\nWhat is the canonical distinction between a durable chat/thread, a harness session, a turn, and a per-turn model execution when no thread is owned by a provider? Specify identity, lifecycle, restart/resume behavior, and what old provider fields mean.
close_reason: Decision resolved: provider-neutral durable turn and on-demand harness execution boundary

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): A thread/chat is the durable product identity and is provider-agnostic. Each user turn creates a durable harness task executed by an on-demand PortLog harness invocation; the invocation may be short-lived, crash, or be replaced. Persisted events and execution state are the recovery source. The model may declare completion, but the harness accepts completion only through the turn's completion policy: deterministic validators, human approval, or explicit terminal response can complete it; policy limits, cancellation, or unrecoverable errors can terminate it as cancelled or failed. No universal HarnessOperationKind is part of the canonical model; the trace records concrete model/tool calls, results, approvals, failures, retries, and model snapshots.

title: Define the canonical harness event and operation trace
description: ## Question\nWhat should SQLite and WebSocket persist and emit for a turn and its agent/tool activity? Compare Pi/OMP and managed-agent event-log patterns; decide whether a generic operation taxonomy is necessary or whether typed tool-call events plus lifecycle metadata are sufficient.
notes: Approved: shared invocation envelope with typed model/tool/logic_program targets; completed deterministic logic-program results replay; durable persistence uses stable invocation IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replay of completed invocations, policy-driven retry/resume, and rebuildable projections.
close_reason: Decision resolved: canonical durable harness trace and payload retention

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Use one invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets for model inference, external tools, and logic programs. They share correlation, lifecycle, timing, retry, and error mechanics but retain distinct execution semantics. No universal HarnessOperationKind. Completed logic-program invocations replay from their recorded result during recovery; interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic invocations may rerun under retry policy.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Durable event persistence uses stable invocation IDs and attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replay of completed invocations, policy-driven retry/resume for interrupted invocations, and projections that can be rebuilt from the event log.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): The canonical trace uses a shared invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets (model, tool, logic_program), stable invocation IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replayable completed invocations, policy-driven retries for interrupted work, and rebuildable projections. Persist semantic event boundaries, checkpoints, lifecycle state, normalized results, and artifact references. Stream transient deltas to the UI but do not persist every token. Do not persist full raw model/tool payloads by default; support optional diagnostic/evaluation capture with retention and redaction controls.

title: Define governed PortLog process actions versus discovered tools
description: ## Question\nFor the initial PortLog architecture, should all capabilities remain generic registry-backed tools, with a future governed-action mechanism introduced only when a concrete process capability needs stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics? Avoid designing a full process ontology now.
close_reason: Decision resolved: generic capability registry and future governed actions

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Initial PortLog uses only generic registry-backed tools. Each tool declares capability scope and policy metadata. A governed domain-action mechanism may be introduced later only when a concrete process capability proves it needs stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics. Do not design a full process ontology now.

title: Specify provider and settings migration to per-turn harness routing
description: ## Question\nHow do existing ProviderKind, provider settings, credentials, model selections, and historical SQLite rows migrate to a global app-default model applied per turn while every agent action runs through PortLog? Define compatibility, fallback, and UI exposure.
notes: Clean-slate target; no legacy compatibility. Global app model default routes every turn through PortLog. Invocation retains standard durable-execution model snapshot and retry/usage metadata.
close_reason: Decision resolved: clean-slate per-turn harness routing and model metadata

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Plan the clean-slate target architecture rather than an enduring legacy compatibility layer. Threads and sessions are provider-neutral; all new turns use the global app model default through PortLog; old provider-owned development data need not remain usable. Credentials remain harness configuration. Each model invocation retains standard durable-execution metadata: resolved model/provider route, relevant settings and configuration version, timing/usage metadata, and retry identity. This is execution metadata only, not thread identity or future routing state.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): The global app default stores a resolved model selection: provider route, model ID, and relevant model settings. Each turn snapshots that selection into model-invocation metadata; threads remain provider-neutral.

title: Define harness authority, approvals, and infrastructure ownership
description: ## Question\nWhich agent-initiated capabilities must be dispatched by PortLog, how are approvals/cancellation/retry/recovery governed, and which responsibilities remain direct server infrastructure (SQLite, WebSocket, settings, projects, user actions)?
notes: PortLog owns complete agent loop; no mandatory human approval gates. Approval-free execution is bounded by scoped capabilities/identity, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, durable recovery, and audit. Need decide PortLog capability/action model.
close_reason: Decision resolved: PortLog authority and capability model

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): PortLog owns the complete per-turn agent loop: model invocation, context assembly, tool selection and dispatch, approvals, checkpoints, retries, cancellation, recovery, and completion. apps/server remains infrastructure and capability adapters; agent-originated effects cross the PortLog authority seam before server execution.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): No mandatory human approval gates. The nuanced authorization, safety, sandboxing, staging, reversibility, audit, and failure-policy design is intentionally delegated to a dedicated research ticket rather than collapsed into 'unconstrained execution'.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): PortLog uses a capability registry plus generic tools. Each tool declares its capability scope and policy metadata; PortLog remains the complete-loop authority and applies deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, recovery, and audit controls. Do not build a full domain-action registry or process ontology yet.

title: Research autonomous PortLog authority without mandatory human approvals
description: ## Question\nHow should PortLog safely and durably govern fully autonomous agent-originated work when human approval is never required by default? Research the user's existing work and relevant patterns for authorization, capability boundaries, sandboxing, policy evaluation, staging/reversibility, auditability, idempotency, failure containment, cancellation, and recovery. Distinguish harness authority from server infrastructure execution. Do not introduce a universal HarnessOperationKind taxonomy.
close_reason: Decision resolved: safety controls for approval-free autonomous execution

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Approval-free autonomous execution is acceptable when bounded by least-privilege capability manifests and scoped identities, deterministic policy gates outside the model, isolation for filesystem/network/process/secrets, idempotency keys for external side effects, explicit unknown outcomes with reconciliation before retry, checkpoints with bounded classified retries and compensation, and append-only audit evidence. Human escalation remains optional rather than a hidden prerequisite. Approval-free does not mean unrestricted execution.

title: Define WebSocket and UI projection for harness traces
description: ## Question\nHow should the provider-neutral durable harness trace be projected to the WebSocket/UI? Define live transient streaming versus durable semantic events, rebuild/reconnect behavior, turn state and invocation rendering, failure/unknown/retry visibility, and how existing orchestration projections are replaced or adapted. SQLite/event log remains authoritative; do not reintroduce provider identity or a universal HarnessOperationKind.
close_reason: Decision resolved: OMP-style WebSocket and UI projection

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Follow OMP-style projection. Conversation remains primary; model/tool/logic-program activity appears inline as expandable details/cards. The canonical typed durable events drive the UI, transient deltas stream live, SQLite/event log remains authoritative, and reconnect rebuilds durable state before resuming live delivery. No separate execution dashboard or universal HarnessOperationKind initially.

title: Implement PortLog as the provider-neutral durable harness
description:
## Problem Statement

PortLog currently sits behind a compatibility bridge in a server architecture whose product model is still organized around provider-specific sessions. That makes the application treat Claude, Codex, OpenCode, and other runtimes as the primary unit of work, even though PortLog's intended product is provider-neutral process engineering. The server must remain responsible for projects, provider-neutral chats/threads, SQLite persistence, settings, WebSocket delivery, and durable history, while every agent-initiated operation is executed through one PortLog harness.

## Solution

Make PortLog the single, provider- and model-agnostic agent harness. A thread is a durable chat identity, not a provider session. Each user message creates a durable turn task and invokes PortLog on demand. PortLog owns the complete agent loop: context assembly, per-turn model resolution, model inference, semantic tool selection, generic tool execution through registered capabilities, logic-program execution, retries, checkpoints, recovery, cancellation, and completion evaluation. Short-lived harness runtimes may be replaced or restarted; persisted turn state and the canonical event log are the recovery source.

The application stores a global resolved model selection—provider route, model ID, and relevant settings—and snapshots it into each model invocation for reproducibility. Existing provider-specific development data is not a compatibility requirement. Credentials remain harness configuration. The UI follows an OMP-style conversation-first presentation with inline expandable activity details.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to start a chat without choosing a provider-owned session type, so that the chat represents my work rather than a vendor runtime.
2. As a process engineer, I want to select a global resolved model default, so that every new turn uses the model configuration I currently prefer.
3. As a process engineer, I want to change the global model default between turns, so that I can use different models for different reasoning tasks without creating a new chat.
4. As a process engineer, I want the selected model and provider route to be captured on each model invocation, so that I can understand what actually produced an outcome.
5. As a process engineer, I want a user message to become a durable turn task, so that work can resume after a process crash or application restart.
6. As a process engineer, I want PortLog invoked on demand for each turn, so that idle chats do not require long-lived harness processes.
7. As a process engineer, I want a turn to resume from persisted execution state, so that completed work is not repeated after a runtime is replaced.
8. As a process engineer, I want the harness to determine when a turn is complete, so that a model stopping its response does not falsely imply that the intended work is finished.
9. As a process engineer, I want deterministic validators, explicit terminal responses, policy limits, cancellation, and unrecoverable errors to contribute to turn completion state, so that completion and failure are observable and trustworthy.
10. As a process engineer, I want the model to choose tools semantically, so that PortLog can support process work without forcing every activity into a fixed operation-kind taxonomy.
11. As a process engineer, I want model inference, generic tool calls, and logic-program execution represented as distinct typed invocation targets, so that each can retain its own execution semantics while sharing lifecycle mechanics.
12. As a process engineer, I want logic-program results to be replayed when already completed, so that deterministic reasoning is not unnecessarily rerun during recovery.
13. As a process engineer, I want interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic invocations to follow target-specific retry rules, so that recovery is safe rather than blind replay.
14. As a process engineer, I want tool capabilities declared in a registry, so that PortLog can expose and govern available capabilities without inventing a complete process ontology first.
15. As a process engineer, I want each generic tool to declare capability scope and policy metadata, so that authorization and deterministic policy checks are enforced outside the model.
16. As a process engineer, I want PortLog to authorize and sequence agent-originated effects, so that the server cannot accidentally become a second agent runtime.
17. As a process engineer, I want server adapters to execute approved harness-directed capabilities, so that infrastructure remains reusable without owning agent decisions.
18. As a process engineer, I want no mandatory human approval gate for normal autonomous work, so that the harness can complete processes without waiting for manual confirmation.
19. As a process engineer, I want approval-free execution bounded by least-privilege identities and capability manifests, so that autonomy does not mean unrestricted access.
20. As a process engineer, I want deterministic policy gates evaluated before dispatch, so that prompts cannot override authorization or safety constraints.
21. As a process engineer, I want tool execution isolated by workspace, filesystem, process, network, and secret boundaries where applicable, so that model-produced actions cannot escape their intended environment.
22. As a process engineer, I want external side effects to use stable idempotency keys, so that retries do not duplicate irreversible work.
23. As a process engineer, I want unknown outcomes distinguished from failures, so that a lost connection after an external effect is reconciled before retrying.
24. As a process engineer, I want checkpoints at durable commit boundaries, so that recovery can resume from the last known safe point.
25. As a process engineer, I want bounded and classified retries with compensation where possible, so that failures do not create uncontrolled loops or inconsistent state.
26. As a process engineer, I want append-only audit evidence for autonomous execution, so that I can reconstruct identity, policy decisions, invocation attempts, effects, and recovery behavior.
27. As a process engineer, I want full raw model and tool payloads excluded by default, so that SQLite growth, sensitive-data retention, and provider coupling stay bounded.
28. As a process engineer, I want normalized semantic events and artifact references persisted, so that durable recovery and useful auditability do not require retaining every raw payload.
29. As a process engineer, I want transient model deltas streamed to the UI, so that responses feel live without storing every token durably.
30. As a process engineer, I want completed message boundaries, tool results, checkpoints, retries, failures, and completion transitions persisted, so that the UI and harness can recover meaningful state.
31. As a process engineer, I want SQLite and the durable event log to be authoritative, so that missed WebSocket messages cannot corrupt the chat state.
32. As a process engineer, I want the UI to rebuild durable state after reconnecting and then resume live delivery, so that an interrupted connection does not lose activity.
33. As a process engineer, I want conversation to remain the primary UI, so that execution details support the chat instead of replacing it with an operations dashboard.
34. As a process engineer, I want model, tool, and logic-program activity shown inline and expandable, so that I can inspect execution when useful without overwhelming the main conversation.
35. As a process engineer, I want unknown, retrying, failed, cancelled, and completed states visible in the activity view, so that the UI accurately communicates durable execution status.
36. As a process engineer, I want projects, chats, settings, persistence, and transport to remain available independently of a running harness, so that the application remains useful infrastructure rather than a collection of provider sessions.
37. As a process engineer, I want future governed domain actions introduced only when a concrete capability needs stronger semantics, so that PortLog can evolve its process ontology from real requirements instead of speculation.

## Implementation Decisions

- Replace provider-specific product identity with provider-neutral threads and durable turns.
- Treat each turn as a durable task whose execution is owned by one PortLog harness implementation and started on demand.
- Keep the harness runtime disposable. Recovery loads persisted turn state and the canonical event log rather than relying on a long-lived process.
- Make PortLog the sole complete agent-loop authority: context, model calls, tool selection, capability dispatch, logic programs, completion, checkpoints, cancellation, retries, and recovery.
- Keep the server as infrastructure: projects, threads, settings, credentials/configuration administration, SQLite mechanics, WebSocket transport, durable projections, and capability adapters.
- Store a global resolved model selection containing provider route, model ID, and relevant model settings. Resolve it at each turn and snapshot it into the model invocation.
- Do not retain a provider-owned thread/session model. Existing provider-specific development data is outside the target compatibility contract.
- Define one shared invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets for `model`, `tool`, and `logic_program`. Do not add a universal `HarnessOperationKind`.
- Give invocations stable IDs and attempt numbers. Make event writes idempotent and append-only. Rebuild current-state projections from the event log.
- Persist semantic event boundaries, lifecycle state, checkpoints, normalized results, policy outcomes, usage/timing metadata, and artifact references. Stream token/delta detail transiently.
- Do not persist full raw model/tool payloads by default. Optional diagnostics/evaluation capture must be separately governed by retention and redaction controls.
- Replay completed deterministic logic-program invocations from their recorded result. Permit rerun only for interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic work under target-specific retry policy.
- Introduce a capability registry for generic tools. Each tool declares scope, policy metadata, input/output contract, execution adapter, idempotency behavior, and applicable isolation requirements.
- Enforce deterministic policy and authorization at the PortLog capability boundary, outside prompts. Use least-privilege capability manifests and scoped identities.
- Keep mandatory human approval disabled for normal autonomous execution. Preserve optional escalation, cancellation, intervention, and policy-based refusal as separate controls.
- Require reconciliation for unknown external outcomes before retry; use stable idempotency keys and durable commit markers for side effects.
- Use isolation, staging, dry-run, compensation, or reversal where the capability supports them; do not claim that every effect is reversible.
- Use SQLite/event log as the source of truth. WebSocket is a live delivery channel only; reconnect rebuilds durable state before continuing live updates.
- Project the UI in an OMP-style conversation-first view with inline expandable activity for model, tool, and logic-program invocations. Do not build a separate execution dashboard initially.
- Adapt existing provider runtime/orchestration consumers through compatibility projections during implementation only where needed to reach the new canonical harness contracts; the target model itself remains provider-neutral.
- Future first-class governed domain actions are deferred until a concrete process capability demonstrates the need for stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics.

## Testing Decisions

- Test the highest seam: submit a user turn through the PortLog turn boundary and observe durable SQLite state plus WebSocket-visible projections. Prefer end-to-end behavior over implementation-specific adapter tests.
- Verify that a turn resolves the global model selection per invocation and records an immutable execution snapshot without making the thread provider-owned.
- Verify restart/replacement recovery from persisted events and execution state, including no duplicate execution of completed invocations.
- Verify typed model/tool/logic-program invocation lifecycles, stable IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent event writes, deterministic replay, and target-specific retry behavior.
- Verify completion policy behavior for explicit completion, validator success/failure, waiting, cancellation, policy limits, unrecoverable errors, and unknown external outcomes.
- Verify capability registry scope and policy enforcement with allowed, denied, malformed, expired, and out-of-scope requests. Tests must prove prompts cannot bypass policy.
- Verify idempotency and reconciliation across timeout-after-effect, duplicate delivery, runtime crash, retry, and compensation scenarios.
- Verify audit output contains normalized attribution, policy inputs/outcomes, invocation attempts, side-effect references, and recovery transitions without requiring raw payload persistence.
- Verify transient streaming is not required for durable recovery, while semantic completion and tool-result boundaries are persisted.
- Verify WebSocket disconnect/reconnect rebuilds the conversation and expandable activity from SQLite/event projections, then resumes live delivery without duplication or loss.
- Verify the UI renders conversation-first output and expandable model/tool/logic-program activity, including retrying, unknown, failed, cancelled, and completed states.
- Reuse existing server integration-test patterns for WebSocket lifecycle, durable event repositories, orchestration projections, provider runtime ingress, and PortLog bridge smoke coverage. Add contract tests at the PortLog boundary rather than duplicating every provider adapter.
- Tests should assert externally observable state transitions, persisted records, emitted messages, and recovery behavior—not private functions, class structure, or the number of internal modules.

## Out of Scope

- Rebuilding the Paper chat design.
- Treating Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, or any other runtime as the product identity of a thread.
- Maintaining a legacy provider-session compatibility layer for nonexistent users or old development data.
- A universal `HarnessOperationKind` taxonomy.
- A full Palantir-style process ontology or domain-action registry at initial launch.
- Mandatory human approval for every agent action.
- Persisting every model token or full raw model/tool payload by default.
- A separate execution dashboard before the conversation-first UI proves insufficient.
- Moving direct user-initiated infrastructure actions through PortLog when they are not agent-originated.
- Replacing projects, threads, SQLite, settings, or WebSocket infrastructure with a harness-owned product backend.

## Further Notes

The target is a clean-slate architecture for an early, not-yet-usable application; preserving old provider-specific development data is not a product requirement. The key design principle is “product on harness, harness on model”: PortLog owns the agent loop and durable execution authority, while the server provides durable application infrastructure and narrow capability adapters. The model supplies semantic reasoning and tool selection, including reasoning through logic programs; the harness supplies execution, policy, recovery, and evidence.

title: Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker
description:
## Problem Statement

PortLog is intended to be a provider-neutral process platform, but its model and credential experience is still organized around legacy provider-specific runtime assumptions. Users need to choose a concrete model through a stable provider access path, yet the current product does not have one explicit contract for provider identity, model membership, credential ownership, availability, authentication state, or selection failure.

This creates several user-facing problems:

- `openai` API access and `openai-codex` subscription OAuth access can expose overlapping model names but are not interchangeable authorizations.
- Related access paths can legitimately expose different numbers of models, as with `xai` and `xai-oauth`.
- Users need to see the full curated catalog, including providers they have not configured, without accidentally selecting a model that cannot run.
- A saved credential is not necessarily valid, and a provider can become invalid later because of an expired subscription, revoked OAuth credential, or rejected API key.
- Credential precedence becomes difficult to understand when runtime overrides, provider configuration, PortLog storage, OAuth, environment variables, and future broker credentials coexist.
- Local tools may need credentials for private repositories, registries, or cloud services, but raw credentials must not be exposed to the model or placed in command-line arguments.

PortLog needs an implementation-ready, provider-neutral catalog, credential, availability, and model-picker contract that mirrors the useful behavior of OMP without depending on OMP's database, configuration schema, or runtime implementation.

## Solution

Build a PortLog-owned provider catalog and credential boundary with an OMP-inspired user experience and explicit PortLog semantics.

PortLog will maintain a human-curated, PortLog-native catalog. Each access path with materially different credentials, entitlements, endpoint behavior, or model membership receives its own provider identity. `openai` and `openai-codex` therefore remain separate provider groups even when their model lists overlap. Each provider owns its model membership, so different providers may expose different counts without requiring artificial parity.

The model picker will group the catalog by provider identity. Providers with a valid API key or usable OAuth credential show a filled green dot. Providers without valid configuration show a gray hollow dot. Their model catalog remains visible for discovery, but model rows are disabled and cannot be selected until authentication succeeds. The main picker uses the visual indicator rather than `Ready` or `Configured` text.

PortLog will use a local, provider-scoped SQLite auth store modeled after OMP's local `agent.db` approach, but with a PortLog-owned location, schema, and lifecycle. The credential-store interface will leave room for a future OMP-style remote broker that keeps long-lived OAuth refresh tokens on a protected host and serves less-trusted or ephemeral clients through authenticated broker operations.

Credential state is durable and provider-scoped. A successful explicit connection test or successful provider use records a persistent last-known-valid state. Definitive authentication or entitlement failures turn the provider gray and disable its models; transient network failures do not invalidate it. If the user's selected provider/model becomes unavailable, PortLog preserves the identity as an unavailable selection, prevents execution, and never silently substitutes another provider or model.

Secret obfuscation follows OMP's design but is opt-in by default. When enabled, PortLog scans environment variables, global/project `secrets.yml` sources, built-in credential-shaped patterns, and registered PortLog credentials. Reversible placeholders are restored only at an authorized local execution boundary. Secret-capable tools declare explicit scopes and channel bindings; the preferred delivery is a controlled environment, stdin, temporary process-only credential file, or provider-specific credential channel, never raw command-line arguments.

The resolved provider/model selection is a global app default captured immutably per turn. Provider credentials remain harness configuration and are never inferred from a thread's provider ownership.

## User Stories

1. As a PortLog user, I want to browse all curated providers, so that I can understand which access paths the product supports.
2. As a PortLog user, I want providers grouped by provider identity, so that `openai` and `openai-codex` are visibly distinct authorizations.
3. As a PortLog user, I want `xai` and `xai-oauth` to appear as separate provider groups, so that their different credentials and model memberships are clear.
4. As a PortLog user, I want each provider to show only its own models, so that provider-specific availability is represented honestly.
5. As a PortLog user, I want providers to expose different model counts when their access paths differ, so that the catalog does not pretend that every credential grants the same access.
6. As a PortLog user, I want the provider picker to show a green dot for a valid API key, so that I can identify usable providers at a glance.
7. As a PortLog user, I want the provider picker to show a green dot for a usable OAuth credential, so that I can identify authenticated subscription access without reading status text.
8. As a PortLog user, I want an unauthenticated provider to show a gray hollow dot, so that I can distinguish a visible catalog from an executable provider.
9. As a PortLog user, I want unauthenticated provider models to remain visible, so that I can discover what becomes available after setup.
10. As a PortLog user, I want unauthenticated provider model rows to be disabled, so that I cannot accidentally select a model that cannot run.
11. As a PortLog user, I want the provider detail view to offer the supported API-key or OAuth setup action, so that I can authenticate without guessing which credential type is accepted.
12. As a PortLog user, I want the main picker to use compact visual state instead of `Ready` or `Configured` labels, so that the catalog remains easy to scan.
13. As a PortLog user, I want the green provider state to persist across application restarts, so that the picker does not forget a previously validated provider.
14. As a PortLog user, I want a revoked OAuth credential to turn its provider gray after PortLog observes the definitive failure, so that the UI does not continue advertising unusable access.
15. As a PortLog user, I want an expired subscription to turn its provider gray after the provider denies access, so that subscription entitlement is reflected in the picker.
16. As a PortLog user, I want transient network errors not to turn a valid provider gray, so that temporary outages do not force unnecessary reauthentication.
17. As a PortLog user, I want a successful connection test to restore the provider's green state, so that I can recover from an invalid or expired credential.
18. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to preserve my unavailable global model choice, so that fixing the credential can restore my intended selection.
19. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to block a turn when the selected provider/model is unavailable, so that an invalid selection cannot enter execution.
20. As a PortLog user, I do not want PortLog to silently switch providers or models, so that a turn never runs under a different authorization, endpoint, price, or capability set than I selected.
21. As a PortLog user, I want the global model default to be captured at turn creation, so that changing the picker later does not change an already-running turn.
22. As a PortLog user, I want `openai/gpt-5.x` and `openai-codex/gpt-5.x` recorded as different concrete identities, so that durable history explains which authorization actually ran.
23. As a PortLog user, I want one active credential per provider in the first milestone, so that initial credential management stays simple.
24. As a PortLog user, I want the credential data model to support multiple accounts later, so that future account selection does not require changing model identities.
25. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog credentials to remain separate from OMP credentials, so that PortLog owns its security and lifecycle boundaries.
26. As a PortLog user, I want provider credentials stored in a local PortLog-owned SQLite auth store, so that the implementation follows a proven local-agent pattern without coupling to OMP internals.
27. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to support native API-key entry, so that providers without OAuth can be configured.
28. As a PortLog user, I want provider-specific OAuth onboarding where it is supported, so that subscription and account-based providers can use their native login flow.
29. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to mask credentials in the UI, so that secrets are not casually disclosed while being managed.
30. As a PortLog user, I want an explicit connection test, so that I can validate a provider before attempting a turn.
31. As a PortLog user, I want turn-start readiness checks to be bounded, so that a stale credential is caught without an indefinite wait.
32. As a PortLog user, I want provider startup to avoid probing every provider, so that opening PortLog does not depend on every external service being reachable.
33. As a PortLog user, I want explicit runtime credentials to override lower-precedence credentials, so that one turn can intentionally use a different credential.
34. As a PortLog user, I want provider configuration credentials to override stored credentials, so that explicit provider configuration remains authoritative.
35. As a PortLog user, I want stored OAuth credentials to refresh before lower-precedence sources are considered, so that subscription providers remain usable without manual token copying.
36. As a PortLog user, I want stored API keys to participate in predictable precedence, so that saved credentials work consistently across sessions.
37. As a PortLog user, I want provider environment variables to remain supported, so that CI and existing local workflows continue to work.
38. As a PortLog user, I want a configured provider API-key value to support OMP-style environment-variable-name-or-literal semantics, so that configuration remains concise.
39. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to distinguish a configured credential from a valid credential internally, so that an invalid key cannot be mistaken for usable access.
40. As a PortLog user, I want secret protection to be available without forcing it on me by default, so that PortLog matches OMP's opt-in behavior.
41. As a PortLog user, I want secret obfuscation to scan environment variables, global/project `secrets.yml`, built-in credential-shaped patterns, and PortLog auth-store credentials, so that common secret sources share one protection boundary.
42. As a PortLog user, I want reversible placeholders for secrets that may safely be restored locally, so that a model can work with redacted context without receiving the raw value.
43. As a PortLog user, I want irreversible replacement for secrets that must never be restored, so that high-risk values remain one-way redacted.
44. As a PortLog user, I want reversible placeholders to remain stable across restarts when possible, so that durable replay does not produce confusing placeholder changes.
45. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to warn if its placeholder key cannot be persisted, so that I understand why placeholders will not be stable across restart.
46. As a PortLog user, I want only explicitly authorized tools to receive a secret, so that ordinary file, status, and read tools do not gain credentials.
47. As a PortLog user, I want secret capabilities to be declared by the tool registry, so that the model cannot invent a credential scope.
48. As a PortLog user, I want secret injection bindings to be defined by the tool adapter, so that the model cannot redirect a credential to an unsafe channel.
49. As a PortLog user, I want secret-capable tools to receive credentials through environment, stdin, temporary credential files, or provider-specific channels, so that raw secrets do not leak through command arguments.
50. As a PortLog user, I want PortLog to record secret restoration and injection decisions without recording raw secret payloads, so that credential use remains auditable.
51. As a PortLog user, I want ordinary autonomous work not to require a human prompt for every authorized secret injection, so that capability-scoped automation remains usable.
52. As a PortLog operator, I want a credential-store interface that can later be backed by a remote broker, so that broker support does not require rewriting adapters or harness logic.
53. As a PortLog operator, I want a future broker to manage both API and OAuth credentials, so that the interface remains general while OAuth refresh-token protection is the primary benefit.
54. As a PortLog operator, I want a future broker to keep long-lived OAuth refresh tokens off ephemeral workers, so that CI and containerized execution have a smaller credential exposure surface.
55. As a PortLog operator, I want provider credentials to remain harness configuration rather than thread ownership, so that the same durable thread can run future turns with different global model selections.
56. As a PortLog operator, I want durable events and projections to retain the resolved provider/model snapshot per turn, so that reconnect and audit views remain accurate even after global settings change.

## Implementation Decisions

- PortLog owns a normalized provider catalog rather than copying OMP's catalog configuration shape. The catalog is human-curated and checked in or otherwise versioned as product data.
- The canonical model identity is provider-scoped: `provider/model-id`. Provider identity is part of authorization and routing semantics.
- A materially different access path becomes a separate provider identity when credentials, entitlements, endpoint behavior, or model membership differ. Overlapping model IDs do not collapse those identities.
- Each provider owns its model membership. Model counts are not expected to match across related providers.
- Catalog presence and execution availability are separate. A visible model is not necessarily selectable or executable.
- The provider picker is grouped by provider identity and shows the full curated catalog. It uses a filled green dot for persistent last-known-valid provider health and a gray hollow dot for invalid, unconfigured, or otherwise unusable provider access.
- The main picker does not display `Ready` or `Configured` labels. Provider detail and onboarding may explain missing or invalid access and provide setup actions.
- Models under a provider without valid access remain visible for discovery but are disabled and cannot be selected. A disabled provider model cannot become the global default.
- Provider health is durable. A successful explicit connection test or successful provider use marks a provider valid. A definitive authentication or entitlement failure marks it invalid. Invalid state disables all provider models until a later successful test or use restores validity.
- Transient transport errors, timeouts, and provider 5xx responses do not invalidate provider health. The adapter must classify definitive authorization/entitlement failures separately from retryable failures.
- OAuth expiry may use the provider's normal refresh path once during an active turn. Failed refresh produces a provider-specific failure and invalidates the provider when the failure is definitive; PortLog never changes provider/model identity as recovery.
- The global model default is app-wide and persisted. Each new turn captures an immutable resolved provider/model snapshot. A thread does not own a provider identity.
- When a persisted selection becomes unavailable, PortLog preserves the selected identity as an unavailable choice for recovery and display, but blocks execution. It never silently falls back to another provider or model.
- PortLog owns a provider-scoped local SQLite auth store with a PortLog-specific schema and lifecycle. It does not read or write OMP's `agent.db`.
- The credential-store interface supports save, remove, resolve, test, refresh, status, and provider-scoped revocation. The first implementation supports one active credential per provider while leaving room for multiple stored accounts.
- The first credential milestone supports native API-key entry, secure persistence, masking, explicit testing, removal, environment-variable support, and provider-specific OAuth extension points. OpenAI API, OpenAI Codex OAuth, and Cursor OAuth are initial access-path targets; other providers may expose only the methods they support.
- Credential resolution follows OMP-compatible precedence: explicit runtime override, provider configuration override, stored OAuth with refresh, stored provider API key, provider environment mapping, broker-migrated/secondary stored credentials, and provider fallback resolver.
- A configured provider `apiKey` first resolves as an environment-variable name and falls back to a literal token when no variable exists.
- Credential configuration is not equivalent to credential validity. The UI uses the provider health indicator rather than exposing verbose status labels in the primary picker.
- The future remote credential broker is an extension of the credential-store interface, not a first-milestone dependency. It may hold API and OAuth credentials, with the primary use case of keeping long-lived OAuth refresh tokens off CI runners, containers, and other ephemeral clients.
- Secret obfuscation is opt-in by default, matching OMP. When enabled, it scans matching environment variables, global/project `secrets.yml`, built-in credential-shaped token patterns, and registered PortLog auth-store credentials.
- Secret protection has reversible `obfuscate` and irreversible `replace` modes. Reversible placeholders use a private per-install HMAC key persisted in the PortLog home directory. If persistence fails, PortLog uses an ephemeral process key and records a visible warning.
- Reversible placeholders are never restored into provider-visible messages, durable transcripts, logs, or replay data. Restoration is limited to explicitly authorized local execution.
- Tools declare secret capabilities such as provider or registry scopes. The capability registry checks policy before any restoration or injection. Secret-capable tools are not prompted on every invocation by default; policy and capability checks are the authorization boundary, and the decision is audited without raw payloads.
- Tool adapters define secret injection bindings. The preferred channels are controlled environment variables, stdin, temporary process-only credential files, or provider-specific credential channels. Raw secrets are not put in command-line arguments.
- Provider adapters own native protocol translation, provider credential use, auth refresh, error classification, and model/tool streaming. The harness remains provider-neutral and receives a resolved model/provider execution target through its per-turn snapshot.
- Server infrastructure continues to own projects, durable threads, SQLite, settings, WebSocket delivery, and durable history. Provider credentials and provider adapters remain infrastructure/configuration behind the PortLog harness boundary.
- The highest implementation seam is the server-side provider availability and turn-selection boundary: it resolves catalog plus credential state into a provider-grouped picker projection and rejects unavailable model selections before a turn enters PortLog. The durable turn path then captures the resolved selection for execution and history.
- The preferred end-to-end verification seam is the PortLog turn boundary: submit a user turn, resolve the global model and provider health, assert durable SQLite state, assert the WebSocket-visible projection, and verify restart/replacement behavior without duplicate execution.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests must assert observable behavior at the highest available seam. They should not assert private helper calls, internal storage layout, or implementation-specific event ordering unless that ordering is part of the external contract.
- The primary seam is a server-side provider/model selection and PortLog turn boundary test. It should exercise catalog grouping, credential health, disabled unauthenticated model selection, valid selection capture, definitive invalidation, and fail-closed turn admission through one public-facing server path.
- The highest durable behavior test submits a user message with a global provider/model selection, then verifies that one durable turn captures the exact provider/model snapshot, that the provider-neutral thread remains provider-free, and that the resulting projection can be rebuilt after a server restart or replacement.
- Provider availability tests should cover green-state persistence after successful test/use, gray-state invalidation after invalid API key, revoked OAuth, expired subscription/entitlement denial, and unchanged health after timeout or 5xx failure.
- Picker projection tests should cover separate provider groups, provider-owned model counts, visible-but-disabled unauthenticated models, selectable authenticated models, and no accidental cross-provider fallback.
- Credential-store tests should cover provider scoping, one active credential, removal, resolution precedence, environment-variable-name-or-literal semantics, OAuth refresh classification, and preservation of metadata without exposing raw secrets in normal projections.
- Secret-obfuscation tests should assert raw values do not appear in provider-visible payloads, transcripts, logs, or replay data when protection is enabled; reversible placeholders restore only for a declared capability and correct binding; undeclared tools receive no raw value; irreversible replacements never restore; and ephemeral-key fallback emits the expected warning.
- Tool capability tests should exercise a generic tool registry through dispatch, confirming that a tool with no matching secret capability cannot receive a credential and that a declared capability binds only to its adapter-defined channel.
- WebSocket tests should verify that provider health and grouped model availability updates are projected consistently, that reconnect rebuilds from durable state, and that a definitive invalidation disables models without requiring a second provider-specific runtime loop.
- Browser tests should focus on user-visible behavior: provider groups, green/gray indicators, disabled unauthenticated model rows, setup affordances, model selection, preserved unavailable defaults, and no silent fallback.
- Prior art includes existing provider health and connection tests, BYOK catalog/model availability tests, provider model-option tests, orchestration command-reactor tests, projection pipeline tests, durable turn/projection persistence tests, WebSocket snapshot/live-stream tests, and browser tests for settings/provider catalog panels. New tests should reuse those seams rather than create parallel provider-specific state machines.
- Deterministic fixtures and fake credential stores/adapters are preferred. Live provider calls, real OAuth accounts, real subscription expiry, and real secret values are not required for the default test suite.

## Out of Scope

- Reusing OMP's credential database, OMP's models.yml schema, or OMP's internal runtime modules.
- Implementing every provider or every OAuth flow in the first milestone.
- Making model lists identical across related providers.
- Runtime synchronization or automatic discovery of the OMP catalog.
- Per-model live smoke tests; trusted documentation and adapter-family fixtures establish tool capability.
- Automatic silent fallback between providers or models.
- Persisting provider identity on a durable thread as thread ownership.
- Requiring human approval for every normal model call, tool call, or authorized secret injection.
- Building the remote credential broker in the first local auth-store milestone.
- Encrypting or redesigning every existing credential store before the PortLog provider boundary is established; at-rest hardening must be resolved before shipping sensitive production credentials but should not expand the picker/turn seam unnecessarily.
- Putting raw credentials in command-line arguments, model context, provider-visible text, durable transcripts, or ordinary logs.
- Defining a universal operation-kind taxonomy beyond the typed model, tool, and logic-program invocation boundaries already required by the harness.
- Replacing projects, threads, settings, SQLite, WebSocket transport, or durable history with provider-owned infrastructure.

## Further Notes

- This specification reconciles the accepted PortLog domain decisions with the existing provider-neutral harness direction. The existing implementation and issue records for the initial harness slices are marked closed, so this should be published as a follow-up implementation-ready issue under the PortLog planning parent and linked to the existing harness implementation issue rather than reopening completed work.
- The primary user-facing contract deliberately uses visual provider health instead of verbose status text. Detail views may still explain why a provider is gray and provide the next action.
- A green dot is a durable last-known-valid signal, not a promise that every future request will succeed. Definitive provider responses can invalidate it; transient failures cannot.
- Provider health and model selection must remain separate from provider runtime session identity. A thread can survive a provider change between turns because each turn captures its own provider/model execution snapshot.
- The model picker should not make users understand credential precedence in order to choose a model. Precedence remains deterministic for operators and diagnostics, while the primary UI communicates only whether the provider is currently usable.
- Secret capability injection is primarily for local tools that genuinely require credentials, such as private repository access, private package installation, cloud CLI operations, or registry publishing. Normal read, edit, status, and test tools should not receive secrets.
- OMP references used for these decisions include its provider picker behavior, local SQLite auth store, credential precedence, secret obfuscation, and remote auth-broker model. PortLog remains the owner of the product contract.

title: Establish the provider catalog projection
description:
## Parent

pl-217.9 — Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker

## What to build

Make the model picker behave like the OMP reference for the unauthenticated catalog state. The user opens model selection and sees every curated provider identity as its own provider section. Each section shows its provider-specific model count and catalog model list. Related access paths such as openai/openai-codex remain separate, and providers are never merged because model IDs overlap. The server exposes this as one provider-grouped projection that the UI can render without inventing provider membership.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The PortLog-native catalog projection contains provider identity, display metadata, provider-owned model membership, model count, and health state.
- [ ] The UI renders every curated provider as a separate section.
- [ ] Provider model counts may differ and are displayed without normalization.
- [ ] Catalog models remain visible for discovery before authentication.
- [ ] No unauthenticated model is selectable.
- [ ] Deterministic catalog, projection, and UI tests cover separate identities and unequal model counts.

## Blocked by

None — can start immediately.
close_reason: Implemented provider-grouped catalog projection, RPC contracts, settings UI, and deterministic tests.

title: Add API-key credential lifecycle and provider health
description:
## Parent

pl-217.9 — Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker

## What to build

Let a user configure an API-key provider from its gray provider section. The detail view offers a masked API-key input and the supported environment-variable path. Saving persists one active provider credential, while an explicit connection test determines whether the provider turns green. A successful test enables that provider's model rows. Removing the credential or observing a definitive invalid-key response turns the provider gray and disables its rows; temporary network failures preserve the last-known-valid state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PortLog-owned SQLite auth storage persists one active API credential per provider behind a credential-store interface.
- [ ] Provider detail supports save, explicit test, remove, and recovery actions.
- [ ] Credential resolution follows the accepted OMP-compatible precedence and environment-name-or-literal behavior.
- [ ] Successful validation persists green provider health and enables model selection.
- [ ] Definitive invalid-key failures persist gray health and disable the provider's models.
- [ ] Transient network and provider 5xx failures do not invalidate health.
- [ ] Deterministic credential-store, health, API, and UI tests cover the full flow.

## Blocked by

- Establish the provider catalog projection
close_reason: Implemented provider-scoped API-key storage, save/test/remove UI, connection probing, durable health, and transient-failure preservation.

title: Add OAuth onboarding and entitlement invalidation
description:
## Parent

pl-217.9 — Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker

## What to build

Let a user authenticate an OAuth access-path provider from its gray provider section. The provider detail offers a native Log in with OAuth action, opens the browser authorization flow, accepts the callback, and stores the provider-scoped credential. The provider turns green and its permitted models become selectable. On later use, the adapter refreshes expired access once. Revocation, expired subscription entitlement, or a definitive refresh failure turns the provider gray, disables its models, and exposes a reconnect action. Logout removes the credential and returns the provider to gray.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] OAuth login, callback, refresh, logout, and invalidation use the PortLog credential-store boundary.
- [ ] Initial OAuth access paths include openai-codex and cursor where their native flows are supported.
- [ ] OAuth identities remain separate from API-key provider identities.
- [ ] Successful OAuth authentication persists green health and enables only that provider's model membership.
- [ ] Definitive revocation or entitlement failures persist gray health and disable model rows.
- [ ] OAuth health persists across restart until definitive failure or logout.
- [ ] Deterministic provider fixtures cover callback, refresh, logout, and entitlement failure.

## Blocked by

- Add API-key credential lifecycle and provider health
close_reason: Completed native Codex and Cursor OAuth login/logout flows, callback completion, configured CLI path support, provider-health refresh, persistent authenticated state, and OAuth UI actions.

title: Enforce authenticated model selection at the PortLog turn boundary
description:
## Parent

pl-217.9 — Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker

## What to build

Make model selection a real PortLog turn choice. The user can select only an enabled model under a green provider. PortLog persists that selection as the global default; when the user sends a message, the server resolves it once and creates one provider-neutral durable turn with an immutable provider/model execution snapshot. If the provider becomes gray later, the prior selection remains visible as unavailable but cannot start another turn. The composer blocks execution and directs the user to restore credentials or select another green provider. PortLog never silently substitutes a model or provider.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gray-provider model rows are browseable but disabled and cannot become the global default.
- [ ] A green-provider model selection persists as the global default.
- [ ] A user message creates one durable provider-neutral turn with the exact provider/model snapshot.
- [ ] Changing the global selection does not mutate a running turn.
- [ ] An unavailable default is preserved for recovery but fails closed at turn admission.
- [ ] SQLite, WebSocket, reconnect, and restart projections preserve the same selection and state.
- [ ] Tests prove no duplicate turn creation and no silent provider/model fallback.

## Blocked by

- Establish the provider catalog projection
- Add API-key credential lifecycle and provider health
- Add OAuth onboarding and entitlement invalidation

title: Add capability-scoped secret protection and local injection
description:
## Parent

pl-217.9 — Define PortLog provider catalog, credentials, and model picker

## What to build

Let a user opt into secret protection and run a credential-dependent local tool without exposing the credential to the model. PortLog registers configured auth-store, environment, and secrets.yml values with the obfuscator. Ordinary tools receive no secret. A secret-capable tool declares its scope and channel binding; PortLog checks policy and injects only the required value through environment, stdin, a temporary credential file, or a provider-specific channel. The UI shows semantic credential-use activity without raw values, and audit data records scope and outcome only.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Secret obfuscation is off by default and can be enabled through PortLog settings.
- [ ] OMP-style secret sources and reversible/irreversible modes are supported.
- [ ] Persisted HMAC placeholders work across restart; ephemeral-key fallback emits a warning.
- [ ] Secret restoration/injection requires a declared capability and uses the adapter-defined channel.
- [ ] Ordinary tools and undeclared tools receive no raw secret.
- [ ] Raw secrets never enter model messages, command-line arguments, durable transcripts, or logs.
- [ ] Audit records contain scope and outcome without raw secret payloads.
- [ ] Deterministic dispatch, obfuscation, policy, and UI tests cover authorized and denied flows.

## Blocked by

- Add API-key credential lifecycle and provider health
close_reason: Implemented opt-in secret protection, persisted HMAC placeholders, capability-scoped channel injection, BYOK message redaction, and secret audit logging.
